reason: Attacked on wording, locator, attribution, scope, format, cap and prior shipping; it holds. Wording: two independent texts print the proverb identically as ‘Eternity is in love with the productions of time.’ The Wikisource transcription of copy D (Blake’s own plate text, with period spellings intact around it: measur’d, wholsom) and the Project Gutenberg text of the 1906 John W. Luce edition, ebook 45315 (modernised spelling elsewhere: plough, wholesome, measured) differ from each other on five of the fifteen neighbouring proverbs but agree letter for letter on this one, so there is no edition drift to exploit and the line is safe in either text. Locator: both texts place it tenth, immediately after ‘He whose face gives no light, shall never become a star.’ and immediately before ‘The busy bee has no time for sorrow.’, exactly as the evidence states; Wikipedia and secondary sources put the Proverbs of Hell that open the series on plate 7, which agrees with the evidence’s parenthetical. Counting proverbs instead of citing a plate is the honest choice here since facsimile plate numbering varies, and it is independently checkable. Attribution: Blake’s own illuminated book, not on the brief’s misattribution list, and not one of the two speaker traps: the Proverbs are collected by the narrator among the fires of hell and are printed under Blake’s own section title, with no named character to credit; the locator already prints ‘Proverbs of Hell’, so the infernal register is on the card. Cap and ban: shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], yearCount 0, atCap false, banned false, so nothing is already in Q, Q_MAKERS, UPLIFT or this file and Blake is clean for the year. Scope: 1790, well before 1999; a named work by a named author, so the out-of-scope line on proverbs and anonymous traditions does not reach it; no scripture, no lyric, no oratory, nothing needing a warning. Format: the source leads with the name, has no dash, is 90 characters, and the quotation ends in a full stop with no straight double quote and no apostrophe to curl. Prose aphorism on a single plate line, so no slash lineation is owed. Tag: Poetry is the right cell in the closed vocabulary for a Blake illuminated book, the only alternatives being Essay or Philosophy, both worse. Two soft points, neither fatal and neither a reason to hold the line. First, the card prints (1790) while the evidence leans on a copy D transcription the Wikisource header dates 1793; the work is conventionally dated 1790 to 1793 and the Library of Congress copy D is captioned 1790, so (1790) is standard shorthand rather than a false claim, but the range is the more exact date and betterCitation offers it. Second, the note is empty: a line about eternity and the productions of time sits a little off June’s truth-and-clarity centre, and a one-sentence note saying the proverbs are spoken in the voice of Blake’s hell, where energy is the good, would earn its place on the card.
